entries.title: The Seljuk Turks
entries.summary: The Seljuks were a Turkic dynasty that dominated much of Iran, Iraq, and Anatolia in the 11th–12th centuries, acting as sultans while recognizing the Abbasid caliph.
entries.detailed_information: The Great Seljuk Empire rose under leaders such as Tughril Beg, who entered Baghdad and became protectors of the Abbasid caliph. Vizier Nizam al-Mulk helped shape administration and madrasa education (Nizamiyya). The Battle of Manzikert (1071) against Byzantium opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement, a key step toward later Ottoman history. Seljuk authority later fragmented into regional sultanates, including Rum in Anatolia.
entries.historical_significance: Transformed the political map of the Middle East and Anatolia; linked to Crusades-era dynamics.
related_questions: How did the Ottoman Empire begin?

entries.title: Battle of Manzikert
entries.summary: At Manzikert in 1071 CE, Seljuk Sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV, accelerating Turkic expansion into Anatolia.
entries.detailed_information: The Byzantine defeat weakened imperial control in Anatolia and is widely seen as a turning point leading to lasting Turkic-Muslim presence in the region. Later political developments eventually contributed to the rise of Anatolian beyliks and the Ottomans.
entries.historical_significance: Strategic turning point for Anatolian history and later Ottoman origins.
